name: Bladder leakage: types and NHS help
summary: The NHS lists stress, urge, mixed and overflow incontinence, and a GP can talk through treatments such as pelvic floor exercises and bladder training.
keyPoints: The NHS describes stress incontinence as leaking under pressure, such as when coughing or laughing, and urge incontinence as leaking after a sudden, strong need to pee.
The NHS advises seeing a GP about any type of urinary incontinence.
Treatments tried first include lifestyle changes, pelvic floor muscle training and bladder training, with medicines and surgery for some people.
NICE guidance for women says clinicians classify the type of incontinence at the first assessment and use bladder diaries.
Sudden loss of bladder control with back pain, numbness or leg weakness is an emergency, and NHS Scotland advises calling 999 or going to A&E.

body.heading: What are the types of bladder leakage?
body.body: The NHS lists several types of urinary incontinence, and they have different patterns. In stress incontinence, leaks happen when the bladder is under pressure, for example when coughing or laughing. In urge incontinence, a sudden, intense need to pee comes first, and urine leaks before the toilet is reached. Mixed incontinence is a combination of the two. Overflow incontinence, which the NHS also calls chronic urinary retention, happens when the bladder cannot empty fully. The NHS also lists total incontinence, which is sometimes described as severe, continuous leaking.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body: The NHS says stress incontinence is usually linked to weak or damaged pelvic floor muscles, or damage to the muscle that keeps the urethra closed. Urge incontinence can come from a problem with the detrusor muscles in the bladder wall, and one NHS trust lists bladder irritation from infection or medicines, nervous system conditions and anxiety. The NHS lists pregnancy and vaginal birth, being overweight, family history, constipation and getting older among the factors that raise the chance of leaks. Some medicines can also affect bladder control, and the NHS says a GP may advise whether changing them could help.

body.heading: What does a GP do when someone asks about it?
body.body: The NHS says urinary incontinence can usually be diagnosed after a talk with a GP. The GP asks about symptoms and may do a pelvic or rectal examination. A GP may also suggest keeping a bladder diary, which records how much is drunk and how often urine is passed. The GP may also check for causes such as a urinary tract infection. The NHS advises seeing a GP for any type of incontinence, so that the type and likely causes can be worked out.

body.heading: What can be done about it?
body.body: The NHS and NHS inform describe simpler approaches as the usual starting point. These include treating an underlying cause, lifestyle changes, pelvic floor muscle training and bladder training. Lifestyle changes can include cutting down on caffeine, and one NHS trust suggests water or decaffeinated drinks in its place. The same trust lists artificial sweeteners, fizzy drinks and alcohol as other possible bladder irritants. One NHS trust says that straining to poo can weaken the pelvic floor muscles. For urge symptoms, a GP may prescribe a medicine called an antimuscarinic if bladder training has not helped. For stress incontinence, a medicine called duloxetine is one option that has been described, and the sources say it should not be stopped suddenly. Pads are not a treatment, but they may be useful while waiting for an assessment or for a treatment to start working. Surgery depends on the type, and the options listed include sling procedures and bulking agents injected near the urethra for stress incontinence.

body.heading: What are pelvic floor exercises and bladder training?
body.body: Pelvic floor muscle training is a programme of exercises for the muscles that support the bladder. The NHS says a GP may refer someone to a specialist, usually a physiotherapist, to start a programme. Bladder training aims to lengthen the gap between feeling the urge to pee and actually going. A pelvic floor programme and bladder training are described as first-line approaches, and they work best when kept up consistently, according to one NHS trust.

body.heading: What does NICE say about women with incontinence?
body.body: NICE has guidance called urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women, which covers the management of both. At the first assessment, NICE says clinicians classify the incontinence as stress, mixed, or urgency or overactive bladder. NICE advises bladder diaries in this first assessment. For urgency or mixed incontinence, NICE names bladder training lasting at least six weeks as the first treatment. NICE also says duloxetine is not a first treatment for women whose main problem is stress incontinence. NICE does not recommend absorbent pads or similar products as a treatment for incontinence. It also says devices placed inside the vagina or urethra are not used for routine management.

body.heading: When should someone get urgent help?
body.body: Sudden loss of bladder control together with back pain, numbness or weakness in the legs can be a sign of cauda equina syndrome, which NHS Scotland treats as an emergency. NHS Scotland advises calling 999 or going to A&E straight away. Blood in the urine is a different matter. The NHS says it is not usually serious but can sometimes be, so it needs checking, and it advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111. Common causes include urinary tract infections, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate. For leaks without these signs, a routine GP appointment is the route the NHS describes.
